az_weeping_wall.blurb: A small bouldering wall on Mount Lemmon in the Santa Catalina Mountains, part of the Cataract Boulders in Bear Canyon. It is the upper of two short cliffs in a gully, about 10 to 12 feet tall and gently overhanging. Five problems run from roughly V2 up to V6, one at each grade. A few pads and attentive spotters are worth bringing. The black and tan stone has an unusual feel for the mountain, and because few people come here the lines can be dirty. The boulders around it sit mostly in shade by early afternoon and stay cool.
az_weeping_wall.parking_note: Use either of the two roadside pullouts near mile marker 9.4 on the Catalina Highway; the right-hand one sits directly below the gully that leads up to the wall.

az_waterfall_dome.blurb: A big dome in the East Stronghold of Cochise Stronghold in southern Arizona, at roughly 5,700 feet. It holds five trad routes, most of them two or three pitches, spanning easy low-angle terrain up to 5.9. The dome is recognisable by a large double roof on its south face. The base is reached partway along the trail toward the Rockfellow group, leaving the main path on its north-east side and crossing slab beneath the roofs. Descent is by a cairned walk-off to the west or southwest over a slab of chickenheads that can be down-climbed.

az_club_med.blurb: A small crag on the Lower Highway section of Mount Lemmon near Tucson, with five routes: four bolted and one trad. Grades start at 5.10 and reach 5.12, mostly 5.10 and 5.11. The cliff is lower than neighbouring Weathertop, and the routes are steep. The bolting is of the older sport style, so you must get your feet above a bolt before reaching for the next. Finding the way down to the base is not obvious and relies on cairns. The Lower Highway setting is Sonoran Desert among large saguaro, and cooler months suit it best.

az_forehand_wall.blurb: The first wall on the left in the Hairpin Turn Area on Mount Lemmon's lower highway, north of Tucson. It has five mostly well-bolted sport lines, running from easy terrain up to about 5.9+, and two of the lines have a second pitch that can be linked or split at a mid-point anchor. The wall faces east and keeps the sun well into the afternoon. The reddish-orange rock is loose and chossy, so belayers should wear helmets. A bee hive is known nearby, and a serious attack has happened. The walk in goes up a wash filled with boulders and sand.
